'''Frederick Justin Almgren Jr.''' (July 3, 1933 – February 5, 1997) was an American [[mathematician]] working in [[geometric measure theory]]. He was born in Birmingham, Alabama.

Almgren received a [[Guggenheim Fellowship]] in 1974.  Between 1963 and 1992 he was a frequent visiting scholar at the [[Institute for Advanced Study]] in Princeton.<ref>According to [[#{{harvid|The Institute for Advanced Study|2012}}|Almgren's Community of Scholars web site Profile]] and to {{harv|Mitchell|1980|p=48}}: the latter reference lists his appointments at the Institute only up to 1978.</ref>

Almgren wrote one of the longest papers in mathematics,<ref>Published in book form as {{harv|Almgren|2000}}.</ref> proving what is now called the [[Almgren regularity theorem]]: the singular set of an ''m''-dimensional mass-minimizing surface has dimension at most ''m−2''. He also developed the concept of [[varifold]],<ref>See his mimeographed notes {{harv|Almgren|1964}} and his book {{harv|Almgren|1966}}: the former one is the first exposition of his ideas, but the book (in both its first and second editions {{harv|Almgren|2001}}) had and still has a wider circulation.</ref> first defined by [[Laurence Chisholm Young|L. C. Young]] in {{harv|Young|1951}},<ref>Young calls these geometric objects ''generalized surfaces'': in his commemorative papers describing the research of Almgren, {{harvs|txt|first1=Brian|last1=White|author1-link= Brian White (mathematician)|year=1997|year2=1998|loc1=p.1452, footnote 1|loc2=p.682, footnote 1}} writes that these are "''essentially the same class of surfaces''".</ref> and proposed them as [[generalized solution]]s to [[Plateau's problem]] in order to deal with the problem even when a concept of [[Orientation (geometry)|orientation]] is missing. He played also an important role in the founding of ''[[The Geometry Center]]''.

Almgren was a student of [[Herbert Federer]], one of the founders of [[geometric measure theory]], and was the advisor and husband (as his second wife) of [[Jean Taylor]].
His daughter, [[Ann S. Almgren]], is an applied mathematician who works on computational simulations in astrophysics. His son, [[Robert Almgren|Robert F. Almgren]], is an applied mathematician working on market microstructure and trade execution.

Almgren died in Princeton, New Jersey on February 5, 1997, aged 63.
